Cite factual sentences using exact supplied physical PDF page markers, for example [PDF p. 31].

Combine the following page-cited section summaries into a coherent narrative of about 650 words.

If evidence is absent, do not fill the gap from memory. These notes are incomplete source representations.
SECTION SUMMARIES:
The Hippodrome’s central spine featured three surviving monuments that outlasted the surrounding walls [PDF p. 51]. The first was a golden tripod dedicated at Delphi in 479 B.C. after the Persian defeat at Plataea [PDF p. 51]. Phocians had stolen its gold six centuries prior, yet inscriptions on its base remained visible to archaeologists [PDF p. 51]. A square bronze column of more modern work stood nearby, contrasting with the ancient artifacts [PDF p. 51]. The Turks now call this open space the Atmeidan, remembering its equestrian past in name only [PDF p. 51]. Along the eastern wall stood chapels and statues, including the Milion milestone of the empire [PDF p. 51]. Constantine contributed a porphyry column topped by a bronze Apollo from Hierapolis [PDF p. 51]. He altered this statue into an imperial image by replacing its head with his own features [PDF p. 51]. This practice mirrored Roman papal actions, where Aurelius was converted into St. Peter on the Corso [PDF p. 53]. North of the Hippodrome stood Constantine’s original church dedicated to Divine Wisdom [PDF p. 53]. This earlier basilica burned twice and left no trace of its initial architectural character [PDF p. 53]. A wooden gallery connected St. Sophia’s west door to the palace Royal Gate [PDF p. 53]. This passage allowed the emperor to attend services without crossing the busy Chalcoprateia street [PDF p. 53]. The author compares this elevated walkway to the corridor linking Florence’s Pitti and Uffizi palaces [PDF p. 53]. These structures formed the city’s heart, hosting most significant historical events [PDF p. 53]. Other notable buildings included the Church of the Holy Apostles and public granaries along the quays [PDF p. 53]. An equestrian statue of Constantine near the praetorian prefect’s palace became a medieval legend site [PDF p. 54].

Constantine chose Byzantium as his capital around A.D. 328 or 329, though exact dates remain uncertain [PDF p. 54]. He consecrated the city on May 11, 330, with Christian bishops blessing the palace and St. Sophia [PDF p. 55]. Although unbaptized, Constantine ensured the new capital was explicitly Christian from its inception [PDF p. 55]. Pagan temples survived only as artistic relics in baths and senate houses, not for worship [PDF p. 55]. To populate the city, he invited senators and wealthy provincials to establish residences there [PDF p. 55]. Artisans received special privileges, while merchants flocked to the new commercial hub [PDF p. 55]. The transfer of Egyptian wheat tribute provided free corn, a powerful but demoralizing incentive for immigration [PDF p. 55]. An edict in 330 named the city New Rome, though people preferred calling it Constantinople [PDF p. 56].

Constantine died peacefully on May 22, A.D. 337, receiving baptism on his deathbed [PDF p. 57]. His realm was divided among relatives until Constantius II consolidated power through murder and war [PDF p. 57]. Constantius II focused on ecclesiastical disputes rather than external threats, initiating Christian persecution of Christians [PDF p. 57]. His successor Julian attempted to restore paganism but failed due to his misguided zeal [PDF p. 58]. Both emperors feared Persian aggression in the east, overlooking dangers from the north [PDF p. 58]. The Goths had been subdued by Constantine between A.D. 328 and 332, forcing them across the Danube [PDF p. 58]. For forty years they settled peacefully, trading with Romans and adopting Christianity under Bishop Ulfilas [PDF p. 60]. Ulfilas translated the Bible into Gothic, creating a vital linguistic relic of Teutonic tongues [PDF p. 60]. The Goths were divided into Visigoths in the south and Ostrogoths in the north [PDF p. 60].

Around A.D. 372, Huns from beyond the Don and Volga invaded Gothic lands [PDF p. 61]. They crushed the Ostrogoths, who became vassals except for a remnant fleeing southward [PDF p. 61]. The Visigoths, led by Duke Fritigern, retreated to the Danube’s southern bank in despair [PDF p. 61]. A contemporary writer describes over two hundred thousand fighting men pleading for Roman protection [PDF p. 62]. Emperor Valens, ruling the East from Constantinople, faced a difficult choice regarding these refugees [PDF p. 62]. He allowed them to cross if they surrendered arms and provided hostages [PDF p. 63]. Roman officials accepted bribes to let Goths keep weapons, violating imperial orders [PDF p. 63]. Governor Lupicinus hoarded food supplies, forcing starving Goths to sell children for bread [PDF p. 63]. An affray at Marcianopolis led Lupicinus to attempt murdering Fritigern during a banquet [PDF p. 64]. The Goths escaped and launched raids across the Balkans, joined by runaway slaves [PDF p. 64]. Initial Roman resistance held them at bay, though battles like Ad Salices proved indecisive [PDF p. 64].

The text presents conflicting evidence regarding the precise date of Constantine’s capital selection, noting it is hard to fix exactly [PDF p. 54]. The author interprets the transfer of Egyptian grain as demoralizing, a subjective judgment not explicitly stated in primary sources [PDF p. 55]. Descriptions of the Huns rely on Gothic historical accounts, which may reflect bias rather than objective fact [PDF p. 61].

The unwarlike Emperor Valens entered the field in person during the following year. He brought great reinforcements from Asia Minor to aid his struggling forces [PDF p. 65]. His nephew Gratian also marched through Pannonia to assist the Lower Danube regions [PDF p. 65]. This personal intervention by Valens resulted in a catastrophic military disaster for Rome. The Goths forced the Balkan line and approached Adrianople in three hundred seventy-eight A.D. [PDF p. 65]

Valens attacked with an army of sixty thousand men near the Gothic encampment. Contemporaries expected victory because Roman infantry still held a reputation for invincibility [PDF p. 65]. However, the Goths had adopted cavalry tactics while dwelling in South Russia and Roumania. They considered fighting on horseback more honorable than engaging on foot during this period [PDF p. 65]

A great body of Gothic horsemen charged the Roman flank unexpectedly during battle. These riders had been foraging at a distance but rushed to the field upon hearing news [PDF p. 66]. The Roman left wing collapsed under the tremendous impact of the mounted assault. Legions and cohorts were pushed together in hopeless confusion by the overwhelming pressure [PDF p. 66]

Roman cavalry abandoned the infantry, leaving them unable to deploy or flee effectively. Soldiers could not raise their arms due to the dense packing of the massed troops. Forty thousand men fell before survivors broke out in a headlong flight from the field [PDF p. 67]. The Emperor and thirty-five commanders died on the battlefield during this fearful defeat [PDF p. 67]

The historian Ammianus Marcellinus compared this slaughter to the ancient disaster at Cannae. The army of the East was almost annihilated and never reorganized on old lines [PDF p. 67]. Victorious Goths subsequently attacked Constantinople but failed due to its vast walls and riches. They abandoned their siege machines and retreated back into Thrace after seeing the defenses [PDF p. 67]

Theodosius succeeded Valens and repaired the disaster through caution and courage combined. He destroyed marauding bands while avoiding direct conflict with the main Gothic body. Peace followed the death of Fritigern, as Theodosius negotiated with his successor Athanarich [PDF p. 68]. The Emperor granted land in Thrace and enlisted Gothic chiefs into his armies [PDF p. 68]

Within ten years, forty thousand Teutonic horsemen served under higher pay than Romans. These auxiliaries won victories for Theodosius against rebel forces in the West later on [PDF p. 69]. Yet this policy placed imperial command effectively in barbarian hands according to the author. It relied solely on personal loyalty and the lingering prestige of Roman culture [PDF p. 70]

The Gothic historian Jornandes recorded King Athanarich’s awe at Constantinople’s grandeur. The king admired the walls, fleets, and disciplined soldiery within the imperial city [PDF p. 70]. This impression did not last long after Theodosius died in three hundred ninety-five A.D. His weak sons Arcadius and Honorius inherited a dangerous political situation [PDF p. 70]

The empire suffered from centralized bureaucracy that suppressed local patriotism and rights. Civil populations were viewed merely as tax sources by the administrative caste officials. Landowners faced restrictions on moving or enlisting without leaving heirs to pay rates [PDF p. 71]. A professional army emerged with no sympathy for the unarmed provincial civilians it protected [PDF p. 72]

Theodosius had swamped native military elements with wholesale enlistment of Gothic war-bands. He handed chief posts to Teutons who were often alien in blood and loyalty. The author argues this created a dangerous guardian class over a timid population [PDF p. 72]

After Theodosius died, factions fought between German and Roman parties at both courts. Stilicho dominated the West as commander-in-chief for the young Emperor Honorius. In the East, Arcadius was weak and controlled by ministers like Rufinus initially [PDF p. 73]. A Gothic captain named Gainas murdered Rufinus before compelling further appointments for himself [PDF p. 73]

Alaric led a Visigothic revolt citing unpaid arrears to the auxiliaries as pretext. He raided from the Danube to Greece while Stilicho blockaded him in Arcadia. The Teutonic minister allowed Alaric to escape, leading to peace and land grants [PDF p. 74]

Alaric ruled parts of the Balkans with undisputed sway for five years thereafter. A German kingdom seemed likely to establish itself permanently south of the Danube then. However, Alaric invaded Italy in four hundred one instead of attacking Constantinople again [PDF p. 75]. Stilicho fought hard but was executed by Honorius on charges of treason shortly after [PDF p. 75]

With Stilicho gone, Alaric moved the Visigoths into Italy to plunder at will. They left the Balkan Peninsula and entered the history of Spain eventually. Meanwhile, Gainas fell out with the eunuch Eutropius in Constantinople’s court politics. He instigated an insurrection under Tribigild to remove his rival from power [PDF p. 76]

Eutropius fled to St. Sophia where Patriarch John Chrysostom protected him temporarily. The preacher used the fallen minister as a sermon illustration on vanity and fate. Arcadius banished Eutropius, but Gainas had him returned and beheaded despite promises [PDF p. 76]

Gainas brought his army to Constantinople to overawe the emperor completely. The author notes that a sack of the city appeared likely at this moment. The text ends abruptly before describing the final outcome of this specific threat. It leaves unresolved how the immediate danger to the capital was ultimately managed [PDF p. 76]

The sudden end of Gainas’s domination resulted from a chance brawl between Goths and citizens at a city gate [PDF p. 77]. This incident triggered a general outbreak against German soldiers in Constantinople [PDF p. 77]. The mob attacked with improvised weapons while closing gates to trap the enemy [PDF p. 77]. Seven thousand Germans died, and survivors fled across the Danube [PDF p. 77]. Gainas was subsequently beheaded by Uldes, King of the Huns [PDF p. 77]. The author notes that Fravitta, a heathen Goth, defeated Gainas in the field [PDF p. 77]. This victory freed Eastern Romans from dual threats of German kingdoms and military dictators [PDF p. 78]. Emperor Arcadius enjoyed seven years of comparative peace following these events [PDF p. 78].

Conflict arose between Empress Aelia Eudoxia and Patriarch John Chrysostom [PDF p. 78]. The empress supported Theophilus of Alexandria against the popular patriarch [PDF p. 78]. A council deposed John, but riots and an earthquake forced his restoration [PDF p. 78]. Hostilities resumed after Eudoxia erected a statue in the Augustaeum [PDF p. 79]. Chrysostom’s sermon comparing her to Herodias led to his banishment in A.D. 404 [PDF p. 79]. His supporters likely burned St. Sophia and the Senate-house in retaliation [PDF p. 79]. John died during exile, leaving a reputation for patience under affliction [PDF p. 79]. The author argues his deposition stemmed from moral clashes rather than ecclesiastical dogma [PDF p. 79].

Arcadius died in A.D. 408, leaving the throne to his seven-year-old son Theodosius II [PDF p. 80]. Minister Anthemius managed the administration with exceptional virtue and ability [PDF p. 80]. He secured a Persian treaty and repelled Hunnish invasions of Moesia [PDF p. 80]. Anthemius also reorganized the corn supply and rebuilt Danube flotillas [PDF p. 80]. Theodosius II grew into an honest but intellectually limited ruler [PDF p. 81]. His sister Pulcheria assumed regency in A.D. 414 after taking a vow of chastity [PDF p. 81]. She ruled successfully for thirty-six years as a crowned nun [PDF p. 81].

Theodosius married the pagan convert Athenais, renamed Eudocia, in A.D. 421 [PDF p. 82]. Tensions between Pulcheria and Eudocia eventually led to the empress’s exile [PDF p. 82]. The author cites a dubious tale involving an apple to explain this breach [PDF p. 82]. Historical records confirm Paulinus was executed and Eudocia retired to Jerusalem [PDF p. 83]. Theodosius faced wars with Persians and Attila the Hun during his reign [PDF p. 83]. Roman armies suffered constant defeats, requiring tribute payments to the Huns [PDF p. 83].

Theodosius II died in A.D. 450 after a fall from his horse [PDF p. 85]. Pulcheria married Marcianus to secure the succession and end Hunnish tribute [PDF p. 85]. Marcianus checked Attila’s advances before the Hun king died in A.D. 452 [PDF p. 85]. Successors Leo I, Zeno, and Anastasius maintained Eastern imperial integrity [PDF p. 85]. The author attributes this survival to capable rulers rather than political conditions [PDF p. 86]. Western emperors became puppets of German generals during the same period [PDF p. 86].

Eastern emperors successfully suppressed ambitious military commanders like Aspar [PDF p. 86]. Zeno and Anastasius overcame rebellions without losing territorial control [PDF p. 87]. The empire remained intact while Western provinces formed Germanic kingdoms [PDF p. 87]. Military reorganization relied on native Isaurian and Armenian troops [PDF p. 87]. This shift reduced dependence on Teutonic auxiliaries in the imperial army [PDF p. 87].

The source presents a narrative heavily reliant on traditional historiographical interpretations. The account of Eudocia’s exile is explicitly labeled as uncertain by the author [PDF p. 83]. The text does not provide primary archival evidence for many political motivations described. Conflicting details regarding the causes of Chrysostom’s deposition are noted but not fully resolved [PDF p. 79].

The final German threat to the Eastern Empire occurred during the reign of Zeno [PDF p. 88]. The Ostrogoths had previously submitted to the Huns ninety years earlier [PDF p. 88]. They regained independence after Attila’s death in A.D. 452 [PDF p. 88]. These Goths replaced the Huns as the primary danger along the Danube [PDF p. 88]. Most settled in Pannonia, bordering Eastern Roman districts [PDF p. 88]. Two chiefs named Theodoric raided Macedonia and Moesia for over twenty years [PDF p. 88]. Zeno attempted to divide them by offering titles and pensions [PDF p. 88]. This strategy failed because the two leaders united against him [PDF p. 88]. One Theodoric accused Rome of using Goths to destroy other Goths [PDF p. 89]. His speech convinced his rival that Roman aid was illusory [PDF p. 89]. They reconciled and fought Zeno together starting in A.D. 479 [PDF p. 89]. Theodoric the One-Eyed died accidentally two years later [PDF p. 89]. His horse threw him against a spear fixed at his tent door [PDF p. 89]. The surviving Theodoric continued to plague the empire until A.D. 488 [PDF p. 89].

Zeno devised a plan to remove this threat by offering Italy to Theodoric [PDF p. 90]. Odoacer had deposed Romulus Augustulus in A.D. 476 [PDF p. 89]. He refused to appoint a new puppet emperor for the West [PDF p. 89]. The Roman Senate asked Zeno to recognize Odoacer as their ruler [PDF p. 89]. Zeno instead advised them to acknowledge Julius Nepos as emperor [PDF p. 90]. Odoacer rejected this advice and proclaimed himself king in Italy [PDF p. 90]. He still nominally recognized the Constantinopolitan emperor as his suzerain [PDF p. 90]. Theodoric accepted Zeno’s offer to conquer Italy from Odoacer [PDF p. 90]. He received the titles of patrician and consul before departing [PDF p. 90]. The Goths defeated Odoacer and established a kingdom at Ravenna [PDF p. 90]. Theodoric professed loyalty to the Eastern emperor throughout his reign [PDF p. 90]. This conquest theoretically reunited the East and West under one ruler [PDF p. 90]. However, Zeno’s actual power in the Western realm remained purely nominal [PDF p. 90].

The Emperor Anastasius died in A.D. 518 at age eighty-eight [PDF p. 91]. Justinus, his body-guard commander, succeeded him with Senate and army support [PDF p. 91]. Justinus was an uncultured soldier who could barely sign his name [PDF p. 91]. He adopted his nephew Justinian as his heir [PDF p. 91]. Justinian was educated in law, finance, theology, and architecture [PDF p. 92]. He showed little personal interest in military matters [PDF p. 92]. In A.D. 526, he announced his intention to marry the actress Theodora [PDF p. 92]. This union scandalized respectable society but pleased gossipmongers [PDF p. 92]. The author notes that libellous accounts of her early life are likely exaggerated [PDF p. 92]. A law forbidding senators from marrying actresses was repealed for this marriage [PDF p. 93]. Justinian’s mother and uncle opposed the union but eventually relented [PDF p. 93]. Theodora was renowned for her beauty despite some physical criticisms [PDF p. 93]. She proved to be a capable and trusted political advisor [PDF p. 93].

Justinus died in A.D. 527, leaving Justinian sole emperor [PDF p. 96]. He ruled for thirty-eight years, dominating the historical period [PDF p. 96]. The empire was prosperous when he assumed power [PDF p. 96]. Anastasius had left a treasury containing over three hundred thousand pounds of gold [PDF p. 97]. The army consisted largely of native subjects rather than foreigners [PDF p. 97]. Heavy cavalry replaced infantry as the primary military force [PDF p. 98]. Foreign auxiliaries like Huns and Herules still served in significant numbers [PDF p. 98]. Financial administration remained weak despite abundant resources [PDF p. 98]. Tax farming and arbitrary customs dues harmed trade significantly [PDF p. 98]. Justinian’s minister John of Cappadocia maintained full treasuries through harsh taxation [PDF p. 99]. This policy impoverished the provinces permanently for future generations [PDF p. 99].

Justinian aimed to reconquer Western territories lost to German kingdoms [PDF p. 99]. He sought to end the pretense of nominal imperial authority in the West [PDF p. 99]. His initial focus involved a four-year war against Persia [PDF p. 99]. The conflict stemmed from rival claims over small buffer states [PDF p. 99].

The source presents conflicting views on Justinian’s character and legacy. It compares him to Louis XIV while noting his superior legal achievements [PDF p. 95]. The text acknowledges the bias of hostile sources like Procopius regarding Theodora [PDF p. 92]. Uncertainty remains about the exact nature of her early life due to libelous accounts [PDF p. 92].
